First, the obvious thing that shouldn't need saying but does: every form of this was an atrocity. Ranking them by suffering is a pointless exercise,  it usually exists only to let one side off the hook (I made this video in reaction to the Asmongold clip but I am sure I could have made a video in reaction to a Muslim downplaying the Trans Saharan trade equally). So I'm not comparing to score anyone. But the differences are worth understanding, because they explain why these systems produced such different worlds afterward.

You were taught the core of it correctly: the boundary really was religious. The criterion was non-belief, not skin — Christians, Jews, Berbers, Persians were all fair game in principle, a Muslim was not. As the older northern sources of captives dried up, the category fell more and more on sub-Saharan Africans. So a religious rule hardened into something functionally racial, exactly as you said.
Some Muslim states avoided spreading Islam into neighbouring lands, because a converted population stopped being a legal supply of slaves. The frontier was worth more pagan.

Where it needs nuance is the conversion escape hatch, which was narrower than it sounds. Converting before capture made you free. Converting after did not — you stayed enslaved, just owed better treatment on paper. 

On sheer brutality, your instinct holds. The Saharan crossing could kill at rates matching or exceeding the Atlantic Middle Passage, and the demand for eunuchs meant field castrations with mortality estimated at 80–90%. Nothing about the Atlantic trade makes that gentler.

The two systems don't diverge in cruelty, and not in intent — both were violent and both were for profit. The difference is structural. Islamic slavery had exits: manumission was a religious virtue, and the child of an enslaved concubine was generally born free. The Atlantic system sealed those exits shut. It made enslavement hereditary and permanent through race, your status passed to your children and theirs, with no theological off-ramp. That's the genuinely new thing. Not that it was crueller in any single moment, but that it was engineered to never end.

reply:
@emilianosintarias7337 I think there are a few different questions getting mixed together here.

First, on the Arab proposal for a unitary state: I think you've got the historical record backwards. The Arab Office representative was Albert Hourani, and before the Anglo-American Committee in 1946 he explicitly argued for a unitary state with an Arab majority and equal citizenship and civil rights for the Jews already living there. The real disagreement wasn't over legal equality but political power. The proposal permanently capped Jewish representation in parliament at one-third and subjected future immigration to an Arab-majority government, which helps explain why the Jewish leadership rejected it. Likewise, I've never found UNSCOP accusing the Arab side of insincerity. Its conclusion was that a unitary state was **impracticable** because two national movements wanted fundamentally incompatible political outcomes, not that one side was secretly lying.

Second, I don't think the "Palestinians only became a people after 1947" argument reflects the mainstream historical literature. Even historians who disagree sharply about the conflict, like Benny Morris and Rashid Khalidi, place the emergence of a distinct Palestinian national movement well before 1947, although they differ on exactly when it became politically mature. Saying that Palestinian identity strengthened after the Nakba is very different from saying it did not exist beforehand.

The bigger issue, though, is your claim that "they weren't asked to lose where they lived." Physically, the plan did not call for mass expulsions. Politically, however, it absolutely required many people to lose sovereignty. Resolution 181 placed roughly 400,000 Arabs inside the proposed Jewish state according to UNSCOP's figures, and later UN analysis that included the Bedouin population put the Arab population at roughly equal to, or even slightly larger than, the Jewish population in that state. In other words, hundreds of thousands of Arabs were expected to become minorities in a state established as Jewish. Whether one thinks that was justified or not, it is hard to argue they "weren't losing anything."

That's also why I think it's important to separate two questions that often get conflated.

Was accepting partition the rational decision? I think the answer is probably yes. Given the regional situation and the prospect of international recognition, the Jewish Agency had strong reasons to accept it. Many historians, including Benny Morris, argue that rejecting it proved disastrous for the Palestinian Arabs.

Was the map itself fair? That's a different question. Plenty of people who were neither Arab nationalists nor anti-Zionists questioned its fairness. The last British High Commissioner, General Sir Alan Cunningham, described it as "manifestly unfair to the Arabs." UNSCOP itself spent considerable time wrestling with the demographic problem of creating a Jewish state containing such a large Arab population. Even Ben-Gurion privately admitted that a state with such a large Arab minority was "not a solid basis for a Jewish state."

So I don't think the regional Arab-Jewish conflict settles the fairness question by itself. It helps explain why the Jewish leadership accepted partition and why many Arabs rejected it, but it doesn't erase the fact that Resolution 181 asked a majority population in much of the territory to surrender sovereignty and become minorities under a new state. Whether that sacrifice was justified is exactly what the fairness debate is about.

reply:
Thank you for the honest engagement. You bring up a lot of points that are really outside the scope of the video, but they're worth going through, so let me give you my take after reading a fair bit of the academic literature on this.

On Jordan first, because it's the big one. It's true that if you count the whole original mandate, most of the land sits east of the river. But Transjordan was carved off back in 1921, twenty-six years before partition, and by 1946 it was already its own independent kingdom under the Hashemites, a family Britain brought over from Arabia. It was never a Palestinian state and it was never run by Palestinians. So the 55% everyone argues about is 55% of what was left, the land west of the river, which is the only part that was ever on the table in 1947. "Jordan is Palestine" is a political argument, not a settled historical fact, and folding it back in is really comparing two different maps.

Syria is a similar move. It was a French mandate settled at San Remo in 1920, and it had nothing to do with what the Palestinian Arabs were or weren't offered, so it doesn't really offset anything.

On the Arabs seeing themselves as part of a wider Arab world, that's fair, pan-Arabism was real and the Arab states did march in in 1948. But you half answer yourself when you say they cooperated terribly, because they did. And it doesn't change the basic fact that the people on that land were the local two-thirds majority who'd lived there for generations. Being part of a bigger Arab world doesn't mean they weren't losing the specific place they lived.

The Arab states did still rejected the plan, they said so openly, and they gambled on a war to stop it rather than take the deal. That's basically Benny Morris's read, and he's not exactly a pro-Palestinian historian. The one thing I'd add is that they weren't offering nothing back. They pushed for a single democratic state with a protected Jewish minority, which from a two-thirds majority's point of view was what they thought fair looked like. They wouldn't negotiate a partition, which is a different thing from having no counter-offer at all.

On them turning down earlier deals too, there's a real pattern there, Peel in 1937, the White Paper in 1939. But it's messier than it sounds. They rejected the 1939 White Paper because it offered them too little for their liking, not because they were handed a state and refused it. So "they kept saying no to a state" isn't quite what the record shows.

The regional point I actually agree with, and it usually gets skipped over. There was no state in the region where Jews ruled Arabs, the reverse was everywhere, and after 1948 something like 800,000 Jews were pushed out of Arab countries. That asymmetry is real and it matters. The only thing I'd flag is that it's an argument about the region and about what you'd expect to happen, not about whether the specific line drawn in 1947 was fair. Those are two separate questions.

And that's really where your last point lands, the ethnostate versus nation-state one. Whether one side would have given its minorities equal rights and the other never would is a claim about how things actually played out over the next seventy years, not something the 1947 plan itself decides. And here's the part people usually miss: the resolution required both states, the Jewish one included, to guarantee their minorities equal, non-discriminatory rights, written into a constitution. On paper, neither side was allowed to be an ethnostate. What each side would actually have done with that is a real debate, but it's a different one than whether the deal itself was fair, so that's the part I'll leave open.

So that's my honest read of it. You're right on the rejection and right on the regional asymmetry, those are strong points. The Jordan and Syria ones don't really hold up, and the equality question is a genuine argument but not one this particular document settles. None of it makes the split fair to the Arabs, and none of it makes it crazy for the Jews either, which is more or less the whole point I was trying to make.
